title: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King
description: The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.L
body: The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.The couple have kept a low profile, but the first picture of Prince Harry since coming back to the UK appears to have been posted on the social media account of Tower Bridge Studios in London.The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals."It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case."The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".Prince Harry and Meghan faced an acrimonious departure from the UK in 2020, which they chronicled in their Netflix documentary.They established their financial independence in California, including Prince Harry writing a best-selling memoir Spare and Meghan creating an online food range, As Ever.This summer the couple made a surprise return to the UK, where their children will be going to school.It's expected that Prince Harry will be supporting his charities, including the Invictus Games, which are due to be held in Birmingham next year.There have been reports that Meghan is considering a return to acting.Disputes about Prince Harry and Meghan's security in the UK remain unresolved and the letter spells out: "Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities."Prince Harry has complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK, but the Palace says that has to be addressed by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - which decides security for royals and public figures.Palace sources have suggested it was better to make the Lord Chamberlain's letter public, in a spirit of transparency, rather than risk it emerging in leaks.Prince Harry and Meghan's representatives have been contacted for a response.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King

title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September."While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.'Significant distress'The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new ownersTwo data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community"."Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

schema.headline: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status

title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
description: Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay
body: Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than £30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other."In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense."The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.Questions are now being asked about if this result could set a precedent across the industry. Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, and Sainbury's are all involved in similar long running claims and will be studying the findings closely.Last year, thousands of female workers at Birmingham City Council heard how much money they will receive in a long-awaited equal pay settlement. Brighton and Hove City Council is also facing over 1,000 equal pay cases.

schema.headline: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling

title: Why the ‘Temu Range Rover’ is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover
description: Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has  travelled down a very rough road.The company has seen sales fall in all
body: Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has  travelled down a very rough road.The company has seen sales fall in all of its major markets and has been dealing with the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year. At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future, in which it is likely to face intense competition from aggressively expanding Chinese brands. Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles. JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.Today, things are very different. The past decade has seen rapid growth among domestic Chinese carmakers, firmly backed by their government, which has been determined to make the country a leading player in electric vehicles. This has created an environment of intense competition, in which local manufacturers have rapidly raised the bar in terms of technology and development speed.That, combined with a slowdown in the Chinese economy and a reduction in sales overall, has made China a much more difficult market for European brands.JLR's Chinese sales fell from a high water mark of 146,000 cars in 2017 to just 62,400 in the last financial year. At the same time, competition and a new luxury car tax have hit profit margins. All of this has resulted in a sharp fall in revenues from the region. JLR is not alone in this; the Volkswagen Group, for example, has also seen its earnings in China pummelled – a major factor in its decision to axe 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade.The state of the Chinese market has had another consequence for European carmakers, including JLR. Faced with cut-throat competition at home, Chinese  firms such as BYD and Chery have been flexing their muscles abroad. They have been rapidly gaining market share in the UK and Europe – with Chery's Jaecoo 7, nicknamed the 'Temu Range Rover'  the third best-selling car in this country over the first half of the year. Analysts say traditional brands will face an uphill struggle to compete with new rivals, who can sell cars more cheaply and develop them more quickly.The US is also a major market for JLR. In the year to the end of March 2025 it sold more than 120,000 cars there. The following year, that figure had fallen to just under 100,000. Part of that could be attributed to the impact of the cyber attack, which heavily disrupted production in late 2025. It affected JLR worldwide and cost the company £1.9bn. But sales and profits were also hit by the introduction of import tariffs by the US, and subsequent uncertainty over the levels of those tariffs. As automotive analyst Matthias Schmidt puts it, the company is "seeing a head-on hit each time a Land Rover rolls off a ship onto US soil".JLR is now planning a partnership with Stellantis to build new Defender-badged vehicles in the US. These cars, which would be developed specifically for the US market, would not attract tariffs.Then, there are energy costs, which affect JLR and its rivals. Carmakers and their suppliers are industrial businesses that use copious amounts of energy, and prices in the UK are among the highest in Europe. According to Prof David Bailey of Birmingham Business School, "electricity is a fundamental input into modern industrial production"."If producing a car in Britain is structurally more expensive because the energy required to manufacture it is substantially more expensive, Britain is effectively imposing a competitiveness tax on its own industry."All of these challenges have come at a time when JLR has been ploughing money into the development of a new generation of electric vehicles. The first fruits of the £15bn programme were seen last week, with the official unveiling of the first electric Range Rover. That was relatively uncontroversial – but so far the relaunch of Jaguar as an all-electric brand has been anything but. In late 2024 the company drove straight into the heart of the culture wars with a polarising advertising campaign that some saw as excessively "woke". The first actual car is due to make its public bow on 6 October – and it will be a pivotal moment for the company.It is easy to see why JLR's chief executive PJ Balaji feels action is necessary to trim costs and make the company leaner. That is bad news for employees, with thousands of jobs to go and compulsory redundancies not being ruled out.But the carmaker's network of suppliers are also being squeezed. "JLR has been pushing hard for cost savings", one leading supplier told the BBC. "But those suppliers are also facing high energy costs and high employment costs…there's huge anxiety right now."

schema.headline: Why the ‘Temu Range Rover’ is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover

title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
description: Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.T
body: Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process."The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save £1.7bn over the next two years.JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack."It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to £22.9bn from £29bn in the previous two years.Why JLR decided change was neededIan Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US."The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party" in terms of electric vehicles. Jaguar launched the I-PACE, a fully-electric SUV, in 2018. But the electric Range Rover announced last week will be its first electric vehicle launch since then.Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".The prime minister's official spokesman said: "We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities."The spokesman added that Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds "is in close contact with JLR and he will be meeting them early this week", but ruled out "any form of bailout".Business and trade committee chair Liam Byrne called the cuts a "body blow for workers, families and communities across the West Midlands". "Whether or not these redundancies are voluntary, we now need urgent assurances that maximum support will be deployed to help everyone affected find new work," he added.Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union would be seeking urgent clarification over the cutbacks, and demanded called for JLR and the government to explore all options to mitigate job losses."Unite will be demanding all necessary levers are pulled to support JLR workers," she said."It cannot be acceptable that workers again are made to pay the price for failings not of their making."Some have blamed the issues facing JLR and the wider UK car industry on the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which was introduced by the previous Conservative government and kept under Labour. It requires that all new car and van sales in the UK must be zero emission vehicles by 2035, but it does not apply to cars sold overseas, which is where JLR makes most of its revenue.Shadow transport secretary Richard Holden said the ZEV mandate and higher energy costs were "crippling the British automotive industry", pledging to scrap the mandate.The UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association has defended the ZEV mandate, previously calling it "crucial for attracting finance into this infrastructure as it sets out a clear, predictable pathway for the growth of the electric vehicle market".

schema.headline: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years

title: Cwmbran man 'pushed off pub stage' before death, inquest told
description: Man, 102, with dementia died after being pushed in pub, inquest toldA 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died ne
body: Man, 102, with dementia died after being pushed in pub, inquest toldA 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died nearly two weeks later, an inquest has heard.Philip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following an incident at the Crows Nest pub in the town on 1 August.He is understood to have been visiting the pub for a drink when he went on to a stage in the venue to complain about the volume of the music.A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains on bail under investigation.The senior coroner Caroline Saunders said the former design engineer "sustained a fall at the pub", adding that it happened "following an allegation that he was pushed".The inquest heard he was taken to the Grange hospital with a fractured hip, however his condition deteriorated and he died on the 12 August.The coroner said Ormerod's death was being investigated by police and that a forensic post mortem examination had taken place.An inquest was opened but adjourned while a police investigation is carried out.The coroner said that the inquest would not be resumed if there was a criminal prosecution, however should there be a need for a conclusion, it would take place on 26 May 2027.Philip Ormerod's son Robert previously said his father was a "pub character" and that he wanted justice for him.Following Ormerod's death, Det Ch Insp Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said a criminal investigation is ongoing and urged people to "consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments" including "online commentary" could have.The force is urging anyone who was at the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 BST on the night of the incident to contact them.

schema.headline: Cwmbran man 'pushed off pub stage' before death, inquest told

title: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow
description: On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshl
body: On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank."We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid."Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April."I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack.Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot."When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him."He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor.The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects.Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched.Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears.Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school.In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot".With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year.The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection."I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades."We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school."But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out.Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react.Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by.Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared."They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village."We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication.All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.  Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village.Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that."At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher – and the number of child injuries is higher too."Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes.A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children, external as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land."And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear".Israel dismissed the report as a "libellous sham".Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children.At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm.Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder."In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have."The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June – and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before."You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said.  "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here."Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said."No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?"The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting."We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes."Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk."Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold."UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher.This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank.All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies.The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt.With Israeli elections less than two months away, Israel's Finance Ministry pushed forward plans this week to take over land registration in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, described by the Israeli settlement monitor Peace Now as "a clear step towards annexation".Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has attributed settler violence to a tiny extremist minority, describing them in a recent television interview as "150 juvenile delinquents".Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026. It says 20 Israelis were killed over the same period, including one child and eight members of the security forces, and 123 Israelis injured.Palestinian parents who have stayed in villages like al-Mughayyir through escalating settler violence are now facing a growing fear of losing their children if they stay on their land.

schema.headline: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow

title: Self-described 'racist monster' Thomas Webster jailed after BBC investigation
description: He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"After BBC contacted X ab
body: He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"After BBC contacted X about the posts, they were taken down - but the company did not comment further.Days before Webster's sentencing, BBC News found another active Substack account appearing to belong to him.The account shared posts discussing Webster's arrest, as well as intimate details of his personal life.It also included several comments about race, including one calling for the "total genetic extinction" of people from South Asia.One comment claimed that these posts were made in spite of bail conditions heavily limiting Webster's internet use and explicitly preventing him from communicating via social media.After the BBC contacted Substack about the content, most of the posts were taken down, although one for which Webster was charged is still visible. The company did not respond further."That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour."Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views."I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't send you to custody."Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech.""Expressing a wish for people to be killed… Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as well… and encouraging other people to express similar views."It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again."Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Self-described 'racist monster' Thomas Webster jailed after BBC investigation

title: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - documentary glosses over the hard stuff
description: "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam. "It's not a
body: "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam. "It's not a power struggle any more."The scene comes towards the end of Don't Look Back In Anger, a sentimental and affectionate portrait of the band's comeback tour in 2025. But it's about as deep as we get into the band's 15-year hiatus. In an opening montage, we hear how Oasis conquered the world in the 1990s with hits like Wonderwall and Roll With It. As their fame grew, so did the brothers' animosity, until the party came to an abrupt halt backstage at a gig in Paris in 2009.Fan shot footage shows the promoter on stage, informing the crowd that the concert is cancelled following "a huge fight together in the dressing room"."The band doesn't exist any more," he announces, sounding more irritated than sad.According to Scottish singer Amy McDonald, who was also on the line-up, the altercation was seismic. "Liam smashed Noel's guitar, huuuge fight!" she tweeted from backstage.The film, however, never tells us what was said. Nobody explains the fall-out. We don't find out who instigated the rapprochement, nor do we hear how it affected their family.Instead, we cut to rehearsals for the comeback tour, with a caption informing us the brothers "didn't speak for 15 years", and an implication that all the wounds have been miraculously healed.Tantalisingly, the first song they practice is Columbia - a fan favourite that never made the tour's setlist - but there's a tension in the room. The band, under Noel's instruction, is piecing together the setlist. Liam won't arrive until later in the process, and no-one's sure which Liam they'll get.When he arrives, he seems fantastically grumpy, complaining about the sound-proofing panels that have been placed in front of Joey Waronker's drums."They're already giving me the hump," he huffs. But when he steps up to the mic, the band relax. Guitarist Bonehead - who's strategically placed between Liam and Noel - beams from ear to ear. A couple of hours later, still in the middle of a song, Liam waves goodbye and casually strolls out of the rehearsal space."I'm not sure whether our kid's enjoying himself," Noel says to his bandmates. In a voice-over, Liam reveals, enjoying himself wasn't the goal."If you're not on it, chaos can ensue," he says, adding that he's given up cigarettes and alcohol (the intoxicants, not the song) for the duration of the tour. "These songs, they need to be treated with the utmost respect."Liam grabs Noel's hand and thrusts it into the air, they launch into the opening chords of Hello, and the crowd practically explodes with joy. As the gig continues, they dance and cheer and weep. During Slide Away, a man sinks to his knees and sings the lyrics, his hands clasped together as if in prayer. When the gig ends, cameras capture a young fan in an awe-struck stupor, unable to tear himself away from his spot on the stadium floor.This is where the documentary excels - capturing the sheer surge of affection that greeted Oasis's return. We visit shows in Dublin, Manchester, Sao Paolo, Tokyo and New York - and every one has a fan with a personal story to tell.One woman has named her dog Bonehead. Another is a Haenyeo - a South Korean free-diver - who says Oasis's music helped her out of depression. Noel, in particular, is blindsided by the impact."The gravity hit me of what it meant to people and it took me by surprise," he reflects. "I have to say it actually knocked me back."Structurally, though, the film has a problem. In a biopic, the triumphant night in Cardiff would have been the final scene - the moment of resolution after 15 years of pain. Here, it comes about 40 minutes into the action. Every subsequent concert just rinses and repeats the same story. The music is still thrilling. The live mix is impeccable. Liam sounds incredible. But  Southern and Lovelace are left flailing around for a story. In Manchester, they focus on a priest delivering a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. In London, they follow a survivor of the Manchester Arena Bombing, who reflects on the way Don't Look Back In Anger became an anthem of resilience.But the film sidesteps the fact that Liam spent the mourning period criticising his brother for his failure to appear at charity shows supporting the survivors.It's not the only omission. There's no mention of the dynamic pricing row that overshadowed the launch of the tour (although Liam is heard apologising for the lack of "cheap seats" during one of the concerts).And while Noel praises Bonehead's contribution to the band, calling him "the sound of Oasis," we never hear from the guitarist; and the film never addresses his cancer diagnosis, which forced him to miss the final leg of the tour.Sometimes, the filmmakers hint at uncovered stories. Noel mentions missing weeks of rehearsals because of a bad back; and its revealed that the Gallagher brothers' kids met for the first time on the tour - but, for some reason, those threads are left un-pulled. Clearly, a decision was made to concentrate on the music. The cameras don't (or weren't allowed to) follow Liam and Noel off stage. Their joint interview provides a few highlights. Liam's riff on Mick Jagger's creaking limbs is worth the price of admission alone. But you get the feeling that everyone's on their best behaviour for Disney Plus... unless you count the copious swearing.That said, if you attended any of the Oasis '25 shows, this is an incredible souvenir of all the tear-soaked euphoria and musical communion that accompanied their comeback.And, of course, it works as a very effective trailer for the band's much-rumoured return to Knebworth next summer.Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger is in cinemas from Wednesday 9 September.

schema.headline: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - documentary glosses over the hard stuff

title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
description: Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.Proposals to merge sma
body: Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government. He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman Zöe Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.In July – just days before Burnham became prime minister – Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

schema.headline: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted

title: Police seek to identify protesters behind Portsmouth anti-migrant disorder
description: Minister condemns disorder at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest after police officers hurtImage caption, Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confront
body:
Minister condemns disorder at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest after police officers hurtImage caption, Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear at the protestByHenry MooreUpdated 3 hours agoPolice are seeking to identify protesters after several officers were injured and vehicles damaged in Portsmouth at a demonstration sparked by the arrival of 120 migrants in a single dinghy.Policing Minister Sarah Jones told the House of Commons the disorder on Sunday night was "intimidating and thuggish" and warned "those who cross into illegality" would "face the full force of the law". The protests followed a large group of masked men holding a demonstration over small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover on Saturday, causing major disruption.Portsmouth City Council said the Home Office had "serious questions to answer" over the decision to bring the migrants, who had crossed the English Channel from France, to shore in the area.Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested. In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest."No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".Figure caption, Watch: Anti-migrant protesters block roads in PortsmouthFootage shared online appeared to show protesters following the convoy of coaches along a motorway after it had left.Protesters said they were trying to stop authorities transporting the migrants to the Manston processing centre in Kent.In a statement to the House of Commons on Monday, the policing minister said: "Peaceful protest is a fundamental part of our democracy and it must be defended But so too is the right of other citizens to go about their lives without undue interference – and there can be no excuse for threatening behavior or serious disruption."Sarah Jones added: "Let me therefore make clear to the House and to the country that disorder of any kind will never be tolerated and those who cross the line from peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law."Responding, shadow home secretary Chris Philp condemned the violence in Portsmouth but added: "This should also be a wake-up call for the government because it's not just those protesters in Dover and Portsmouth who feel so angry about large-scale illegal immigration."It is millions and millions of people up and down this country who feel angry as well."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the country is on the edge of "serious civil disturbance" and called on protests to remain peaceful.In a video posted to social media, he said: "Peaceful protest: good. Uniforms and masks: bad. Voting is the only way we get a solution."
                                
                                                                
                                                                        
                                                                        
                                                                        
                                                                    
                                                                    
                                                                
                                                        
                                    Tap the questions below
                                
                                    
                                        How many people cross the English Channel in small boats?
                                    
                                                Between 1 January and 6 September 2026, a total of 17,138 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.
                                                These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.
                                                Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.
                                                Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.
                                                Boats that arrived in the UK from 7 September 2025 to 6 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.
                                                Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).
                                                When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.
                                                The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.
                                                    
                                    
                                        Who is arriving in the UK on small boats?
                                    
                                                People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.
                                            
                                                                            
                                                                                    
                                                                                    
                                                                                    
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                            
                                                                    
                                                In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.
                                                    
                                    
                                        How else do people stay in the UK without permission?
                                    
                                                Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.
                                                There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.
                                                The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.
                                    Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, who represents Gosport near Portsmouth, accused the Home Office of failing to provide local officials with details of Sunday's protest."As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension," she said.The Labour MP for Portsmouth North, Amanda Martin, said the "emergence" of the route across the Channel taken in Sunday's crossing was "deeply worrying for my city".Some 625 migrants on eight boats were brought to shore at Dover and Portsmouth on Sunday, according to Home Office figures.A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September - which is 43% lower than the same period the previous year.UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012.This weekend's disruption comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.But while the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".In August, a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.It is thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

schema.headline: Police seek to identify protesters behind Portsmouth anti-migrant disorder

title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
description: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose
body: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos."Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely. It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years. "Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th". OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock?This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.  "The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said. Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas.Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility.In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances.The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK.This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history.In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it.The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration.The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him.Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said.Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises

title: OpenAI chief scientist warns no-one is prepared for consequences of AI
description: OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has called for "extreme caution" over AI's runaway progress and warned more intervention may be needed to ensu
body: OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has called for "extreme caution" over AI's runaway progress and warned more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future"."I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," he wrote in a blog post entitled "An Alien Mind, external".The post comes only a few days after the ChatGPT-maker released its latest model GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.OpenAI and other AI firms like Anthropic shared reports of their AI agents acting autonomously and carrying out real-world cyber-attacks on other companies.In July, OpenAI called an incident in which its AI agents - AI systems which can operate alone after human instruction - hacked the tech platform Hugging Face "unprecedented".Meanwhile in September a report claimed months earlier AI agents from the firm had also hijacked a German website."We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity," Pachocki wrote in the latest blog post.He said OpenAI would continue to "build defensive systems" and seek technical solutions to alignment - a term used to describe ensuring a machine's actions and goals perfectly match human intent and safety guardrails.Pachocki added one of the firm's main priorities moving forward would be to build an "automated AI researcher" to keep pace with AI progress while ensuring ways that human researchers could remain part of the process. "Instead of better AI guardrails, regulations, or assurance to keep people safe, they propose developing internal AI agents to research these problems," said Professor Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge."Such answers to growing concerns about the problems OpenAI's models are causing for cyber-security, job loss, mistakes, errors and fraud are simply not good enough."Nathan Calvin, general counsel at the advocacy group Encode AI, said he agreed with Pachocki on the hazards present in advanced AI model development - but he claimed OpenAI was unwilling to be transparent, and said this meant warnings risked being dismissed as "just self-interested hype"."If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution," he wrote on X, external.

schema.headline: OpenAI chief scientist warns no-one is prepared for consequences of AI

title: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return
description: Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed. The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake
body: Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed. The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles for the feature film, with production starting on Monday.The Inbetweeners 3 will follow on the story of their characters, Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper.They originally starred in three seasons of the popular coming-of-age sitcom, which aired on E4 between 2008 and 2010.It followed their trials and misadventures as suburban teenagers at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life and friendship.The show has gained new fans over the years due to some of its best bits finding new life on social media, as well as through the film sequels.The third instalment follows two sequels backed by Film4, which were released in 2011 and 2014. Alongside the announcement, Netflix released a teaser video which showed Will, Simon, Neil and Jay return to their iconic yellow Fiat. The friend group all get into the tiny car but Simon struggles to start the engine. After some encouragement, it gets going and they drive out of what looks like a storage unit. Production kicks off after months of speculation that there would be another film, but beyond the lead characters returning, the rest of the cast is yet to be confirmed. Fans will be wondering if English actress Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D'Amato.However, Netflix has announced The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film.Beesley and Morris said it has been "super fun" hanging out with friends again. "We're going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans," they added. The first film sees the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post sixth form break, but they quickly find more trouble than they bargained for. The 2014 follow-up reunites Will, Simon, and Neil as they travel to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year - where they find out his travels aren't as lavish as his messages had claimed.Tensions rise as they clash over whether to chase cultural experiences or a wilder time on their trip.  The first film made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix, while the sequel also broke box office records.

schema.headline: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return
